Ophthalmology · published research

Orbital implant exposure

One randomized comparison reports faster conjunctival healing with helium–neon laser than with drugs plus surgery in patients with exposed hydroxyapatite implants. A newer mechanistic study also combines an implant model with endothelial-cell experiments, but clinical evidence remains unreplicated.

Summary of the Evidence

Two publications are listed in the exact orbital-implant category. One randomized clinical comparison included 70 patients and a parallel rabbit experiment; the second describes a treated hydroxyapatite implant model and separate endothelial-cell assays. The clinical report concerns exposure of hydroxyapatite implants and should not be generalized to all orbital implant complications.

Human and clinical evidence

Xu et al. randomized 70 patients with exposed hydroxyapatite orbital implants to helium–neon laser or drugs plus surgery (35 per group). Conjunctival wound healing occurred in 34 of 35 patients (97.14%) in the laser group and 26 of 35 (74.29%) in the comparator group (P < 0.05). In mild exposure, the reported healing times were 7.22 ± 2.11 versus 14.33 ± 3.20 days; in moderate-to-severe exposure, they were 18.19 ± 2.12 versus 31.25 ± 4.21 days. This is one clinical publication, with no independent clinical replication listed (Xu et al. 2015).

Animal evidence

The Xu et al. publication also describes 24 New Zealand white rabbits with orbital implants, with tissue and imaging findings interpreted as increased implant vascularization and reduced inflammation after treatment. The newer mechanistic publication reports an LLLT-treated hydroxyapatite implant model and vascular-tissue sequencing (Wu et al. 2025).

In-vitro evidence

In the Wu et al. study, separate assays used rabbit microvascular endothelial cells. The experiments linked miR-90 and VEGFA to cell proliferation, migration, and tube formation; these mechanistic results do not measure conjunctival healing in patients (Wu et al. 2025).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The human protocol used a continuous-wave 632.8-nm helium–neon laser, reported here as 633 nm, for 15 min daily over ten days. The clinical comparison and preclinical models address different outcomes. The positive clinical signal applies to the studied hydroxyapatite implants and comparator regimen; other implant materials, severities, and surgical practices may differ.

Interpretation

The randomized comparison is an encouraging clinical signal supported by preclinical observations, but it comes from one clinical publication. Independent controlled studies are needed to confirm the healing advantage, evaluate complications, and test whether the protocol generalizes to other orbital implants.

Clinical effect sizes (estimate)

Xu et al. (2015) reported healing in 34/35 patients (97.14%) with He-Ne laser and 26/35 (74.29%) with drugs plus surgery (P < 0.05). This is one 70-person comparison in hydroxyapatite implant exposure.

Evidence strength (estimate)

One randomized comparative signal for conjunctival-wound healing.

Laboratory evidence only for cellular angiogenesis.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

The positive clinical result comes from one 70-patient randomized comparison and has no independent clinical replication. The parallel rabbit arm and a newer mechanistic paper add preclinical support, but they do not provide additional patient outcomes or establish generalizability across implant types.
